reader_notes: Idiomatic British reportage - the kind of long-form trade piece ELF actually draws on. The technical register ('scope', 'sinker', 'swivel', 'a floating aid is fixed to nothing; it is moored') is used the way a practitioner would use it, and each term is glossed in passing rather than explained at the reader.
The opening and closing frame (buoy 43 lifted at twenty past six, back over the side by nine, deck hosed down) does real work: it makes the argument in the middle feel observed rather than assembled.

q2 is the best item in the unit. It asks for the mechanism, not the fact, and B is the same idea with the sign reversed - more chain means a wider circle, not a tighter one. A reader who half-understood scope will pick B.

q3 could look like it has two readings: A (marked positions were already uncertain before loggers) and D (the old keepers watched their position more closely than today's crews). D falls away because the text never sets the keepers against present-day crews - it uses them to date the uncertainty, and Fewtrell's quote ('We knew the shoal was under us. Where we were over it was another question') is about the problem, not about diligence. I settled on A without lasting doubt, but D is the closest call in the six units.
q4 rewards reading the concession precisely: Cadell moved on the inshore aids and not on the outer stations. A ('given it up') and C (causal story about the storm) are both clean overreaches.

The penultimate paragraph is unusually honest for a synthetic passage - it says outright that neither record settles the question (two losses in ten years is too thin a series, no grounding traced to the wander). That is what makes q5's B, with its 'unsettled argument', the only defensible main-idea option.

Numbers hold: thirty-one metres of chain in eleven metres of water is a scope consistent with the argument that follows, and 214 aids on a three-year cycle matches the three years buoy 43 has been down.
